newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Trade sees bumper Argentine wheat despite drought.
newsitem.headline: Trade sees bumper Argentine wheat despite drought.

text.p: Drought still lingered over the northern reaches of Argentina's wheat belt Thursday, but traders were doggedly optimistic about the chances of a good 1996/97 crop.

"The thing is that 80 percent of the wheat area is in very good shape, while 20 percent is not in such good shape. But everyone is talking more about the 20 percent than the 80 percent," one trader said.

While the northern dryness has led him to lower his forecast, he said that he still thought output could hit the government's forecast of 15 million tonnes, although it might only make 14.5 million tonnes.
Another trader was estimating 14.3 million tonnes. "We don't think the damage is as bad as some people are saying. There is dryness, there is nervousness, but we don't think there is damage."
Other, gloomier traders said farmers will struggle to scrape together 14 million tonnes of wheat.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Wednesday forecast wheat production will be 14 million tonnes, up from what it said was 8.6 million tonnes last season.
The local Agriculture Secretariat thinks 9.2 million tonnes was produced in drought-blighted 1995/96.

Wheat exports are set to more than double last season's four million-odd tonnes. Traders are concerned that Argentina's transport and storage infrastructure will be seriously stretched, pushing costs up and local prices down.

"Argentine wheat prices could end up divorced from the rest of the world during harvesting. If the price difference with U.S. wheat is $20, this could broaden" one said. But he added, "If Argentina manages to place most of its wheat on the FOB market in the next two months, the situation won't be a catastrophe."
But export sales are going slowly as big buyers hold back to see how long the bearish tendency in world wheat prices can go on for.

"The Brazilians still haven't bought a kilo. We are still hoping for the Chinese and other big destinations to come along," a trader said. "I'd say that 500,000 tonnes would be an optimistic figure for FOB sales so far."

The maize crop is likely to take more of a battering than the wheat if the dry spell drags on throughout September. After bad experiences with early sowing last season, many farmers are determined to hold off planting until it rains.

The USDA said it expects maize output to jump to 12.5 million tonnes from 10.66 million tonnes last season. These compare with the Argentine government's estimates of 12.9 million tonnes this year and 10.5 million tonnes in 1995/96.

Rains forecast throughout Argentina's grains belt for Sunday and Wednesday may improve matters, but areas such as the north of Santa Fe province and Cordoba province are lacking in soil moisture. All is well in the bumper wheat areas of Buenos Aires.
